hints: Look closely at each disc in both dishes. Where do you see a white clear zone with no grey bacteria, and where do you see grey bacteria growing right up to the disc?
Remember that a clear zone means the bacteria were killed or stopped, so they are sensitive. No clear zone means they kept growing, so they are resistant. Think about what the N disc is for.
walkthrough:
**Observe what grew where**

Look at the grey shading, that is the bacterial lawn. A white ring around a disc is a clear zone where no bacteria grow.

For bacteria P, both X and Y have large white clear zones. N has no clear zone. For bacteria R, Y has a white clear zone, but X and N have no clear zone.

**Apply the rule for sensitivity and resistance**

A clear zone means the antibiotic worked, so those bacteria are sensitive to it. No clear zone means the bacteria kept growing, so they are resistant to it.

So P is sensitive to both X and Y. R is sensitive to Y but resistant to X.

**Understand the role of N**

N has no antibiotic, so it is the control. It checks that the bacteria can grow normally on this agar when no drug is present.

In the R dish, bacteria grow right up to N, and also right up to X. This proves R can grow fine, and that the clear zone around Y is really due to antibiotic Y, not a bad plate.

options.A: This reverses the biology. Bacteria can be resistant to antibiotics, antibiotics are not resistant to bacteria.
options.B: Bacteria P show large clear zones around both X and Y, so they are sensitive to both, not resistant.
options.C: Bacteria R show a clear zone around Y, so they are sensitive to Y, not resistant. We also cannot prove a mutation from this test alone.
options.D: N is the no-antibiotic control. It shows grey bacterial growth right up to the disc, proving R grows normally when antibiotic Y is not present.
